title: Basie's New York arrival and the Roseland opening
summary: They discuss Hammond polishing the band, additions to the Kansas City group, and a rough opening night.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Did Claude Williams not satisfy, or did he want to go home or something?
I don't know. I don't know what happened then.
Yeah.
I don't know the reason for [crossed out: byra]. -
Well let me see -- hazard a guess, too. John was very busy polishing up everything, wasn't he?
Mm hmm.
You see, Basie came in with this mystique, and what-not. And, you know, so there were two schools of thought, weren't there?
Mm hmm.

There were people who were thrilled and dying and positive this was going to be terrific -- this breath of something real that swung and just made it it's business to get on with it, you know, and not bother with the fine points, and not bother with being commercial, or anything else, but just going to get on with their business. And there were people who were thrilled about that -- looking for that. But, there were a whole lot of other little schools of people who were ready to say "Now" -- and then find out what was wrong with it, and pull it to pieces, and down it if possible, even, you know, and sweep it out, more or less. And, of course, John was well aware of that and he was going to take care of the soft points -- the places where people could jump on it.

But surely, [crossed out: it had been my feeling] -- that when it came in they had made additions -- made additions to the Kansas City Band, to bring it up to the normal strength. That's how I understood it. You know, when it left Kansas City it was ten or eleven pieces. Then when it [crossed out: came to] played the Grand Terrace they built it up to fifteen.
The Grand Terrace or the Roseland.
No.
The Grand Terrace. They stopped in Chicago. Didn't they stop there on their way?
Oh, yeah.

That's when Fletcher gave them alot of arrangements. But some of the guys that had been put in there to beef it up were not all top notches, and I think by the time they get it into New York, John was quite rightly madly trying to --

Well, I think John was right, no question. And, to tell you the truth -- I think Freddie will bear me out on this -- The fact was that the opening night alot of people thought it was quite scandalous. Do you remember that? There was alot of adverse talk -- all out of tune and Basie had his back to the audience totally --
Where -- where was this?
The Roselord
No.
Oh. You weren't even there? Oh.
See, I didn't go to the do The Roselord.
Well, Basie was so scared that he wouldn't even look at the audience.
I know he was scared.
(laugh) He had his piano fixed so he had a solid back facing the people. (laugh) And, the dance floor, you know. And, he wouldn't even look at people. And, the band was playing -- supposedly
the band was playing out of tune, and it was very rough, and this and that, -- and people said "Oh, dear", you know -- that didn't live up to things --
Mm hmm. Mm hmm.
But, I was there that night, and it was wonderful, --
Mm hmm.
-- and it did swing like mad --
Mm hmm.

-- and it was wonderful. And, people naturally just took advantage of whatever they could -- the rough points, and they were going to say this -- and then, of course, you know, give John credit. He did find some strengths -- and he found you and put you there -- and gee that was important for Basie. Very.
Mm hmm. Mm hmm.
Wasn't Earle Warren in the band when it came east?
No.
Wasn't there someone named [Corky] Roberts?
Coughy.
Coughy.
Yeah. Coughy Roberts.
When they came east I don't think Earle was in there.
Huh?
Was Earle Warren in the band?
No, no, no.
